newsitem.title: USA: Chinese dissident to speak in U.S. next week.
newsitem.headline: Chinese dissident to speak in U.S. next week.

text.p: Chinese dissident Wang Xizhe is in "a safe place" and plans to give a news conference in San Francisco next week, a spokesman for a group which helped him leave China said on Tuesday.

Wang, 46, fled to Hong Kong from his home in China's Guangdong province over the weekend, just days after authorities in Beijing arrested pro-democracy activist Liu Xiaobo and ordered him to serve three years in a labor camp.

Ming Wong, a spokesman for Alliance for a Democratic China, a pro-democracy group which said it helped Wang leave China, declined to say whether Wang was in the United States, but he said he was not in China or Hong Kong.
"He is in a safe place. I couldn't tell you where he is now," Wong told reporters at an Oakland news conference.

He said Wang would speak publicly for the first time since leaving China at a news conference in San Francisco on Oct. 21. He said he did not know the reason for the secrecy, but said Wang needed time to rest. Wang was "very, very tired," he said.
Wang's wife Su Jiang, contacted by telephone from her home in the southern city of Guangzhou, said earlier that friends of her husband had told her he was safely in the United States.
In Washington, a State Department spokesman said Wang was heading for the United States but would not give any other information, saying he was respecting Wang's request for privacy.
The Chinese government has accused Wang of crossing the border illegally and has said Chinese authorities were pursuing those who helped him.
"I hope the Beijing government does not bother his family, his wife and his son," said Wong, who described himself as an old friend of Wang's.
He would not comment when asked whether Wang would apply for political asylum in the United States.
Wang and Liu recently wrote a letter demanding the impeachment of President Jiang Zemin for violating the constitution by placing the army under Communist Party, rather than state, control.

After Liu's arrest, Wang left the country because he feared being arrested too, Wong said. In the past, Wang had never wanted to leave China. "He kept telling us that he wanted to stay in China," Wong said.
Wang's activism dates from 1974 when he co-authored an attack in Guangdong on the radical 1966-76 Cultural Revolution.

He took part in the 1979 Democracy Wall movement in Beijing and produced his own dissident newsletters. He was twice imprisoned and spent some 17 years in jail and labor camps. He was released on parole in 1993, and before he fled he had been under constant police surveillance.
